facts.statehood_note: Minnesota Territory was formed March 3, 1849, and became the 32nd state in 1858.
facts.nickname: The North Star State (also the Gopher State and the Land of 10,000 Lakes)
facts.motto: L'Étoile du Nord (French: The Star of the North), the only state motto in French

symbols.name: Wild rice (manoomin), which the Ojibwe hold sacred

facts.name_origin: From the Dakota name for the Minnesota River: mní sóta, 'clear blue water,' or Mníssota, 'cloudy water.' Dakota people showed early settlers the meaning by dropping milk into water. The state seal includes the Dakota phrase Mni Sóta Makoce, 'the land where the water reflects the skies.'

government.chambers: Minnesota Senate (67 members, usually 4-year terms) and Minnesota House of Representatives (134 members, 2-year terms); legislators have no term limits
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), elected with a lieutenant governor. The governor leads the executive branch and works with the Legislature at the State Capitol in Saint Paul.
government.courts: Minnesota Supreme Court (7 justices, a chief justice and six associate justices), elected to renewable six-year terms; the Minnesota Court of Appeals, created in 1983, handles most appeals first.
government.local: 87 counties, plus cities and townships; cities may adopt home rule charters if voters approve.
government.constitution: Adopted October 13, 1857, shortly before statehood, and amended many times since.
government.kid_line: "Government is instituted for the security, benefit and protection of the people, in whom all political power is inherent." (Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The Dakota lived in what is now Minnesota when Europeans arrived. Many Dakota people consider Bdote, where the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers meet, a sacred place of creation; people have gathered there for at least 10,000 years.

The Ojibwe moved into Minnesota from the east and at first formed an alliance with the Dakota. They hold wild rice sacred, believing the Creator gave it to them; it grows in lakes of central and northern Minnesota.
Around 1000 CE, the Oneota and other Siouan-speaking peoples formed the Upper Mississippian culture, which lasted until Europeans arrived in the 1600s.
Between about 200 and 500 CE, the Laurel people lived in the north and Hopewell communities lived in the Mississippi River Valley in the south.

today.nation: Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians
today.about: A federally recognized Ojibwe nation in northern Minnesota.
A federally recognized tribe made up of six Ojibwe bands: Bois Forte, Fond du Lac, Grand Portage, Leech Lake, Mille Lacs, and White Earth.

first_peoples.today_note: Minnesota has 11 federally recognized reservations: seven Ojibwe and four Dakota. After the 1862 war, many Dakota people were forced out of the state, and Dakota descendants also live in South Dakota and Canada.
sites: Bdote and Historic Fort Snelling, Saint Paul area, where the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers meet; sacred to many Dakota people
Pipestone National Monument, where Indigenous people have quarried red pipestone for prayer pipes for more than 3,000 years; affiliated with 23 tribal nations
Jeffers Petroglyphs, southwestern Minnesota, carvings in Sioux quartzite rock, some matching Dakota designs and some much older

history.event: People are gathering at Bdote, where the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers meet.
Indigenous people begin quarrying red stone at Pipestone to make pipes for prayer and ceremony, a tradition that continues today.
The Oneota and other Siouan-speaking peoples build the Upper Mississippian culture.
French voyageurs and fur traders arrive, using the Grand Portage. Trade pressures help break the Dakota-Ojibwe alliance and lead to war between the two nations.
The United States buys the land west of the Mississippi River in the Louisiana Purchase.
After Zebulon Pike bargains with Dakota leaders for land at Bdote in 1805, the U.S. Army builds Fort Snelling there.
Harriet Robinson and Dred Scott, both enslaved, marry at Fort Snelling, where slavery was illegal. Their years on free soil later become the basis of their freedom suits.
Minnesota Territory is created on March 3.
Under the Treaty of Mendota, Dakota leaders give up most of their lands in Minnesota and Iowa to the United States.
The U.S. Supreme Court rules against Dred and Harriet Scott; they are freed later that year by people who held them. Minnesota adopts its constitution on October 13.
On May 11, Minnesota becomes the 32nd state.
Minnesota offers 1,000 soldiers to the Union right after Fort Sumter; the 1st Minnesota fights at Bull Run, Antietam, and Gettysburg.

After treaties took most Dakota land and hunger spread, the U.S.-Dakota War is fought for six weeks. Hundreds of settlers are killed; afterward about 1,600 Dakota women, children, and elders are held at Fort Snelling, and 38 Dakota men are hanged at Mankato in December.

Dakota people are exiled from Minnesota to the Crow Creek Reservation. On October 2, in the Treaty of Old Crossing, the Red Lake and Pembina Ojibwe bands sign away about 11 million acres in present-day Minnesota and North Dakota.

On November 3, after failed votes in 1865 and 1867, Minnesota voters approve removing the word "white" from the voting rules in the state constitution, giving Black men and other men of color the right to vote. Minnesota and Iowa were the first Northern states after the Civil War whose voters approved this. Women still could not vote.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Robinson Scott
trailblazers.text: Brought enslaved to Fort Snelling, she married Dred Scott there. In 1846 she and Dred filed separate freedom suits, the only married couple to do so; though the Supreme Court ruled against them in 1857, the family was freed that same year.

trailblazers.name: Taoyateduta (Little Crow)
trailblazers.text: A Mdewakanton Dakota leader born about 1810 in the village of Kaposia, he negotiated and signed the 1851 Treaty of Mendota and signed the Treaty of 1858. In 1862, as his people faced starvation and tension with government agents and traders, he agreed to lead Dakota fighters in the U.S.-Dakota War, though many Dakota opposed the killing of settlers. He was killed on July 3, 1863.

trailblazers.name: Charles Eastman (Ohíyesa)
trailblazers.text: Born in Minnesota to a Santee Dakota family, he became a physician on reservations and one of the best-known Native authors and speakers of the early 1900s. He founded 32 Native American chapters of the YMCA and worked for Native rights.

trailblazers.name: Rosalie Wahl
trailblazers.text: In 1977 she became the first woman on the Minnesota Supreme Court, serving about 17 years. She led the state's task forces on gender bias and racial bias in the courts.

trailblazers.name: Mee Moua
trailblazers.text: Her Hmong family fled after the Vietnam War and came to the United States as refugees in 1978. She became a lawyer, served in the Minnesota Senate from 2002 to 2011, and later led a national Asian American civil rights organization.

landforms: Iron Range (Mesabi, Vermilion, and Cuyuna ranges)
Canadian Shield rock in the northeast
Red River Valley, the old bed of glacial Lake Agassiz
Driftless Area bluffs in the southeast
Northwest Angle, the only part of the lower 48 states north of the 49th parallel
geography.regions: Four ecological provinces: prairie parkland in the south and west, eastern broadleaf forest (the Big Woods), tallgrass aspen parkland in the northwest, and the Laurentian mixed forest of the north.

ecosystems.name: Northern Laurentian mixed forest
ecosystems.about: Pine and spruce mixed with birch and poplar; Minnesota has the largest timber wolf population in the lower 48 states, plus moose and black bears.

ecosystems.name: Lakes and wetlands
ecosystems.about: About 10.6 million acres of wetlands, more than any state except Alaska. Lakes hold walleye, northern pike, and muskellunge, and about 12,000 common loons live in Minnesota.

ecosystems.name: Prairie
ecosystems.about: Tallgrass prairie and oak savanna once covered the south and west, but nearly all of it has been broken up by farming and building.

ecosystems.name: Voyageurs and the Boundary Waters
ecosystems.about: In Voyageurs National Park, beavers and fire change the land, and auroras shine over rocks 2.7 billion years old.

science.weather: Very cold winters and hot summers: the record low is −60°F at Tower (1996) and the record high is 114°F at Moorhead (1936). Blizzards, thunderstorms, hail, derechos, tornadoes, and straight-line winds happen, and droughts come every 10 to 50 years.
science.resources: Timber, farming, and railroads built the early economy, and flour mills at St. Anthony Falls ground much of the nation's grain. Iron ore from the Mesabi and Vermilion ranges has shipped from Duluth since the 1880s; today health care, finance, and services lead.
science.highlight: Minnesota has some of Earth's oldest rocks, gneisses about 3.6 billion years old, and near Hibbing a triple watershed sends rain to the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean, or Hudson Bay.

g3_sci.plan: Learn how wolves, moose, and beavers live in the northern forest.
